newsitem.title: USA: CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR PLANS TO VETO PARTS OF BUDGET.
newsitem.headline: CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR PLANS TO VETO PARTS OF BUDGET.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson said on Tuesday he would veto parts of the state budget just passed by the legislature to pressure Democrats who control the body to pass an education bill he supports.
The California legislature passed a $68 billion state budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year on Monday after the second-longest budget deadlock in the state's history.
On Tuesday, the legislature passed most of the several dozen "trailer" bills needed to implement the budget.

But the Democrat-controlled legislature recessed for a summer break until August 25 without taking action on a bill that Wilson, a Republican, wanted passed. The bill would allow students in public schools to be given an assessment test.

Wilson had previously threatened to veto the entire budget if the bill was not passed. On Tuesday, he said he would sign the budget but veto parts of it to pressure Democrats in the legislature to pass the education bill.
"I intend to sign the budget and to withhold certain portions as an incentive," Wilson told reporters.
"We need to be assured we are getting something for our investment," he said, referring to the rise in educational spending contained in the budget.
Wilson, who has line-item veto power, did not say which part of the budget he would veto or when he would sign it.
The state legislature is expected to take up the education bill when it returns after the summer break.
Wilson wants a single statewide assessment test in English only. Democrats want students who are not proficient in English to be able to take the test in their native language.

State Senate President Bill Lockyer, a Democrat, said he felt Democratic leaders and Wilson had reached agreement on 90 percent of the issues involved in statewide testing, but a few key issues remained to be resolved.
"There's no fundamental disagreement. We need more time to work it out," he said.
